newsitem.title: UK: Blair watched by Thatcher, Major in Downing Street.
newsitem.headline: Blair watched by Thatcher, Major in Downing Street.

text.p: When Tony Blair moves into the prime minister's official residence, 10 Downing Street, he will have to pass Margaret Thatcher and John Major on the way to work every morning.

Major's last act after more than six years as as prime minister will be to present a photograph of himself to the new occupants of Number 10. The 50th in the series, it will take its place at the top an original 18th century staircase, pushing Thatcher down a step.
Blair, who is 44 on Tuesday and has a young family, could find the apartment at the top of the grand, terraced house a tight fit despite the acres of official rooms on the floors below.

The Blairs live in a Georgian period house in Islington, a partly gentrified area of north London that is home to many politicians, actors and journalists and one of the natural habitats of moderate New Labour.

The Blairs could decide to move next door to the more spacious Number 11, traditional residence of the finance minister, which has a connecting door to number 10. Gordon Brown, certain to be Blair's choice as Chancellor of the Exchequer, is single.
In the 18th and 19th centuries, chancellors often lived in number 10 while the prime minister of the day kept his office there but lived in his London home or on his country estate.
In the past 120 years, Lord Salisbury in the 1880s and 1890s is the only prime minister never to have lived there.
What is certain is that Blair, wife Cherie -- a high-flying lawyer -- and children Euan, Nicholas and Kathryn will not follow the Majors' example and spend weekdays apart.
Norma Major preferred to stay at their country home in Huntingdon, in the county of Northamptonshire north of London, while John was at his day job.
"Wherever Tony goes, we are going too. The most important thing is to keep the family together," Cherie said before the election. "We want to keep life as normal as possible."

Originally built on wooden foundations, the black-bricked house leans into the central London street, which is closed to the public because of security concerns. Number 10's last private resident was a Mr Chicken.
The Blairs will no doubt want to make their mark on number 10 which has been home of the prime minister since 1735 when Sir Horace Walpole, Britain's longest-serving premier, moved in.

Until the 20th century, prime ministers used to bring their own bedclothes, crockery and furniture when they moved in. But when Ramsay McDonald, a widower, took over in 1924 his eldest daughter began the tradition of buying furniture for the house.
The house has since become a showcase for British art and furniture. Major chose only one "foreign" picture, a Corot, for number 10 which is sprinkled with Constables and Turners.

Blair is a big fan of Renaissance artist Piero della Francesca for his paintings' "strength, humanity and depth of feeling" and is also keen on post-impressionism. He will be able to call upon the Tate and National galleries to fill the house.
Norma Major had a stairlift installed in number 10 to help disabled people but the Majors' biggest impact on the house was in the garden, which holds special memories for John.

They asked for a rose walk to be grown and for climbing plants to conceal the high garden walls. The cherry tree in the garden was given by a national newspaper to replace one destroyed in an IRA mortar attack on Number 10 in 1991.

The rose garden was also the venue for Major's surprise announcement in June 1995 of a ballot for the leadership of the Conservative Party to stop sniping by anti-Europe rebels. He won the internal party vote easily in a two-way contest against rightwinger John Redwood, who stepped down as minister for Welsh affairs to run.
